evidence.claim: Stage roads and a railroad grade link gold towns through winding canyons.
evidence.quote: The Gold Belt Tour follows historic railroad and stagecoach routes

evidence.claim: Stage roads and a railroad grade link gold towns through winding canyons.
evidence.quote: The Shelf and Phantom Canyon Roads cut along unpaved routes through winding canyons.

evidence.claim: The Gold Belt Tour makes a three-legged loop: narrow gravel on Phantom Canyon Road, an unimproved Shelf Road and paved High Park Road.
evidence.quote: The byway forms a three-legged loop with the Phantom Canyon Road (narrow gravel), the Shelf Road (narrow unimproved), and the High Park Road (paved).

evidence.claim: CDOT lists 131 miles and five hours of driving.
evidence.quote: Length: 131 miles Driving time: 5 hours

evidence.claim: A National Scenic Byway since 2000, the tour follows the historic railroad and stagecoach routes that the Federal Highway Administration highlights alongside fossil sites and gold camps.
evidence.quote: National Scenic Byway, 2000

evidence.claim: the tour follows the historic railroad and stagecoach routes that the Federal Highway Administration highlights alongside fossil sites and gold camps.
evidence.quote: The Gold Belt Tour follows historic railroad and stagecoach routes leading to North America's greatest gold camp, three world-class fossil sites, and numerous historic sites.

evidence.claim: The 1890s gold boom underlies the route’s story.
evidence.quote: Colorado’s greatest gold boom in the 1890s underscores the Gold Belt Tour story.

evidence.claim: Shelf Road was built in 1892 for stagecoaches and wagons paying a toll; one stretch hangs 200 feet above the stream bed.
evidence.quote: Shelf Road was a toll road constructed in 1892 for stagecoach and wagon travel. One stretch of Shelf Road clings to a canyon wall 200 feet above the stream bed.

evidence.claim: Phantom Canyon carried ore and mining supplies by rail, climbing 4,550 feet in 30 miles.
evidence.quote: Phantom Canyon Road was once a railroad route moving gold ore and mining supplies. The route climbs 4,550 feet in elevation over a short 30 miles

evidence.claim: Trains added a helper engine at Cramer and took water at Adelaide to make the climb.
evidence.quote: Cramer was a stop where the train added a Helper engine to help pull the train uphill. Adelaide station stop kept a water tank for the train to refill its steam engine.

evidence.claim: The loop takes in Florissant and Cañon City, with High Park Road crossing cattle-ranch country and views toward Pikes Peak.
evidence.quote: The route loops by the Royal Gorge Bridge, Cañon City, Florissant and Florence.

evidence.claim: From Cañon City, Garden Park lies to the north; Shelf Road runs through Fourmile Canyon.
evidence.quote: Located 10 km (6.2 mi) north of Cañon City

evidence.claim: After the mining town of Victor, Phantom Canyon provides an unpaved return toward Cañon City.
evidence.quote: an unpaved road connecting Cañon City and Victor.

evidence.claim: with High Park Road crossing cattle-ranch country and views toward Pikes Peak.
evidence.quote: High Park Road views are expansive and open, dotted with historic cattle ranches. Distant views of the Sangre de Cristo Range to the southwest and Pikes Peak to the northeast

evidence.claim: Shelf Road runs through Fourmile Canyon.
evidence.quote: Shelf Road is a portion of the byway going through Fourmile Canyon

evidence.claim: Mining continues in Cripple Creek and Victor.
evidence.quote: The journey passes through historic Cripple Creek and Victor, where gold mining continues today.

evidence.claim: Garden Park’s name comes from vegetables grown for Cripple Creek miners in the 19th century.
evidence.quote: the name originates from the area providing vegetables to the miners at nearby Cripple Creek in the 19th century.

evidence.claim: Its Jurassic dinosaur discoveries became part of the Bone Wars, with both Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope making major finds here.
evidence.quote: known for its Jurassic dinosaurs and the role the specimens played in the infamous Bone Wars of the late 19th century.

evidence.claim: Four Mile Creek cuts through sedimentary rocks, exposing the Morrison Formation in the canyon.
evidence.quote: The region is bisected by Four Mile Creek (also called Oil Creek), which has carved a canyon through the Mesozoic and Paleozoic sedimentary rocks.

evidence.claim: The dinosaur sites now form the Garden Park Paleontological Resource Area, overseen by the Bureau of Land Management.
evidence.quote: The dinosaur sites now form the Garden Park Paleontological Resource Area, which is overseen by the Bureau of Land Management.

evidence.claim: with both Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope making major finds here.
evidence.quote: Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope both produced major finds here.

evidence.claim: exposing the Morrison Formation in the canyon.
evidence.quote: One of these Mesozoic strata is the Morrison Formation, which is exposed within the canyon.

evidence.claim: In Victor, a building foundation became a gold mine.
evidence.quote: In 1894, the Woods brothers discovered gold when they began digging the foundation for a building, which resulted in the creation of the Gold Coin Mine.

evidence.claim: The Woods brothers struck gold while digging in 1894, creating the Gold Coin Mine.
evidence.quote: In 1894, the Woods brothers discovered gold when they began digging the foundation for a building, which resulted in the creation of the Gold Coin Mine.

evidence.claim: Five years later, a five-hour fire destroyed the business district.
evidence.quote: In August 1899, the business district was destroyed in a five-hour fire.

evidence.claim: Many historic buildings date to that rebuilding year, 1899.
evidence.quote: As a result, many of the historic buildings date to 1899

evidence.claim: The town’s surviving mining equipment includes shaft elevators and mine carts repurposed as flower planters.
evidence.quote: shaft elevators (which carried the miners down), mine carts (now employed by the town as flower planters)

evidence.claim: On the hillsides, tall gallows frames hold the old elevator pulleys that served the mines.
evidence.quote: Several towering 'gallows frames', which house the antique elevator pulleys, can be seen on the hillsides.

evidence.claim: Look for gallows frames on the hillsides, with their old elevator pulleys.
evidence.quote: Several towering 'gallows frames', which house the antique elevator pulleys, can be seen on the hillsides.

evidence.claim: The town’s surviving mining equipment includes shaft elevators and mine carts repurposed as flower planters.
evidence.quote: shaft elevators (which carried the miners down), mine carts (now employed by the town as flower planters), barred tunnels, two outbuildings (an office overlooking the entrance and the building from which the miners set out), and other sites of interest from that era still stand.

evidence.claim: Eight Mile Creek formed Phantom Canyon; the Florence and Cripple Creek Railroad made it a route for gold and supplies.
evidence.quote: The canyon is formed by Eight Mile Creek. The Florence and Cripple Creek Railroad developed it as a route to take gold and supplies in and out of the Cripple Creek and Victor gold mining district.

evidence.claim: The road now follows that railroad route, unpaved between Victor and Cañon City.
evidence.quote: an unpaved road connecting Cañon City and Victor.

evidence.claim: Its engineering included two tunnels cut through granite without timber supports and the Steel Bridge, built in 1897.
evidence.quote: Construction included two tunnels cut through granite rock (no timber supports needed!). Many bridges were built, including Steel Bridge, in 1897.

evidence.claim: The former ore railroad climbed 4,550 feet over 30 miles.
evidence.quote: The route climbs 4,550 feet in elevation over a short 30 miles

evidence.claim: CDOT describes the road as narrow and rugged in places.
evidence.quote: Both Phantom Canyon and Shelf Road are narrow and rugged in places.

evidence.claim: CDOT prohibits vehicles over 25 feet on Phantom Canyon Road and recommends four-wheel drive on Upper Shelf Road.
evidence.quote: 4WD recommended on Upper Shelf No vehicles over 25 feet long on Phantom Canyon Road

evidence.claim: The road now follows that railroad route
evidence.quote: Phantom Canyon Road was once a railroad route moving gold ore and mining supplies.

evidence.claim: Mining continues in Cripple Creek and Victor. On the canyon roads, CDOT notes narrow, rugged stretches; on the paved High Park leg, historic cattle ranches occupy open country.
evidence.quote: The journey passes through historic Cripple Creek and Victor, where gold mining continues today.

evidence.claim: On the canyon roads, CDOT notes narrow, rugged stretches; on the paved High Park leg, historic cattle ranches occupy open country.
evidence.quote: Both Phantom Canyon and Shelf Road are narrow and rugged in places. High Park Road views are expansive and open, dotted with historic cattle ranches.

evidence.claim: The valley itself forms a triangle, bounded by cliffs on two sides and mountains to the north; the dinosaur sites extend onto and along those cliffs.
evidence.quote: Garden Park proper is a triangular valley surrounded by cliffs on the southeast and southwest and by mountains to the north; however, the name is also refers to the dinosaur sites on top and along the cliffs.

evidence.claim: Victor housed most of the miners working the district’s 500 mines, while mine owners and investors lived in neighboring Cripple Creek.
evidence.quote: Mine owners and investors lived in Cripple Creek, while most of the miners for the districts' 500 mines lived in Victor.

evidence.claim: At Adelaide, a water tank replenished steam engines; at McCourt Station, telegraph messages helped manage train movements along the route.
evidence.quote: Adelaide station stop kept a water tank for the train to refill its steam engine. To manage train travel, telegraph messages were sent from McCourt Station.

flags: CDOT lists 131 miles and five hours; archived FHWA lists 135 miles and six hours including loops or backtracking. CDOT figures used.
The route is a three-legged loop. Moments follow Cañon City north via Garden Park and Shelf Road to Victor, then return via Phantom Canyon; strip towns give sparse anchors.
Driving restrictions are checked against the saved CDOT page only; no live access check was possible.
Current claims were supported; Jack Dempsey and the museum-held Stegosaurus were omitted for focus, not lack of evidence.
